subject: Anthropology
title: Language Acquisition
description: Learn Language Acquisition in one minute.

hook.text: No one teaches babies grammar rules. Yet by age four, every child speaks in full sentences. How?

buildup.text: Children acquire language through immersion, not formal instruction. They absorb patterns from speech around them.

discovery.text: Noam Chomsky proposed a universal grammar — an innate brain structure that makes language learning possible.

twist.text: Anthropologists argue social interaction, not biology alone, drives acquisition. Kids learn language by using it.

climax.text: Language acquisition blends biology and culture. The brain is wired for language, but culture provides the content.

punchline.text: Nature gives the capacity; culture fills it.

quiz.question: What did Chomsky propose about language?
options: Humans have an innate capacity for grammar

details.summary: Children acquire language through a combination of innate cognitive capacity and social interaction. Cross-cultural research shows that while the biological capacity is universal, the social context of language learning varies enormously and shapes communicative competence.
details.whyItMatters: Language acquisition reveals the interaction between biology and culture. All children learn language, but how they are taught and what communicative norms they learn vary dramatically, shaping lifelong social behavior.
takeaways: Language acquisition combines innate capacity with social interaction
All children acquire language but learning contexts vary cross-culturally
Communicative competence includes cultural norms beyond grammar

faq.question: Do all cultures teach language the same way?
faq.answer: No. Western middle-class parents often simplify speech and narrate children's actions. Many other cultures expect children to learn by observing rather than direct instruction. Some cultures rarely address preverbal infants directly. All approaches produce competent speakers.

faq.question: What is communicative competence?
faq.answer: Beyond grammar, children must learn when to speak, when to stay silent, how to address different people appropriately, and how to interpret indirect meaning. This cultural knowledge about language use is communicative competence, and it varies as much as grammar across cultures.
